offence_severity: Death (Section 302) and Robbery (Section 397) - Minimum 7 years, Maximum Life Imprisonment
physical_harm: Injuries on head of a 90-year-old lady resulting in her death
number_of_offences: Three counts charged (Sections 302, 397, 449), two upheld (Sections 302 and 397)
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused did not have premeditation for murder but had planned robbery
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-2 (Lidiya), the 11-year-old daughter of the victim, was accepted by the court as credible due to her direct experience as a victim of the crime and the traumatic nature of the events. The court also relied on the medical evidence showing the victim's injuries were caused by the accused and the recovery of stolen items from the accused.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, particularly PW-2, as having higher credibility due to her status as a victim of the crime and the traumatic nature of the events. The court emphasized that the evidence of such a victim should be placed on a higher pedestal than that of other witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 20th October 1997; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court decision: 30th October 2007; Supreme Court decision: 21st November 2012
legal_representation: Purnima Bhar for the Appellant; Liz Mathew, Sana Hasmi for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced; High Court: Upheld conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, acquitted of charge under s. 449 IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused dragged down a frail old lady of 90 years from her cot and caused injuries on her head with a wall clock, which resulted in her death. They also contended that the accused had gone to the house for the purpose of committing robbery and not to kill anyone.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the absence of a Test Identification Parade (TIP) made the evidence of the victim unreliable. They also contended that the accused had no intention to murder the deceased and, therefore, his conviction for an offence punishable under Section 302 was improper.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the failure to hold a TIP is not fatal to the prosecution's case, but the trial judge must be circumspect in accepting the identification of an accused by a witness in court if the accused is a stranger to the witness. The court also emphasized the importance of victimology and the treatment of victims in the administration of justice.
precedent_relied_upon: Sk. Hasib v. State of Bihar, AIR 1972 SC 283; Vaikuntam Chandrappa v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1960 SC 1340; Rameshwar Singh v. State of J & K, 1972 (1) SCR 627 = (1971) 2 SCC 715; Budhsen v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1971 (1) SCR 564 = (1970) 2 SCC 128; Malkhansingh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2003 (1) Suppl. SCR 443 = (2003) 5 SCC 746; Vijay@ Chinee v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 2010 (8) SCR 1150 = (2010) 8 SCC 191; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Lekh Raj, 1999 (4) Suppl. SCR 286 = (2000) 1 SCC 247; Bikau Pandey v. State of Bihar, 2003 (6) Suppl. SCR 201 = AIR 2004 SC 997; State of Rajasthan v. Kishore, 1996 (2) SCR 1103 = AIR 1996 SC 3035
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the accused was found guilty of murder and robbery with the intent to cause death, but not for house trespass with the intent to commit an offence punishable with death.
